subject: grayWolf
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: gray wolf standing alert.
Style: Blizzard/Warcraft.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module for a stylized, Warcraft-style gray wolf model standing in an alert pose—exaggerated proportions, chunky shoulders, thick fur ruff—figuring out proportions like shoulder height and body length before writing the code.

Now I'm sketching the joint hierarchy: a hips root joint, a spine chain curving forward through mid-body to the withers and neck base, then a neck/head/jaw chain, plus a tail chain branching back from the hips. For the body mesh, I'm planning to loft a surface over the spine chain's stations, skinning it to that chain so the geometry follows the skeleton naturally.

I'm working out actual coordinates now, aiming for a stylized wolf with raised head, roughly 1.2m to the top of the head and about 1.1m body length, sketching shoulder/hip heights and chest/waist/hip cross-section dimensions, then laying out spine path points from rump through hips, waist, ribs, to chest and into the neck base.

For the joint hierarchy, I'm deciding the hips joint acts as root with the spine chain starting there, then adding a neck chain running from the base of the neck up to the head, parented off the last spine joint, with the path broken into a couple of segments for neck1/neck2 joints.

Then for the head itself, I'm placing a head joint aimed forward with a slight downward tilt so the wolf looks alert, and figuring out how to build the skull shape using a loft along the head bone from back to nose.

Plotting station points for skull back, brow, muzzle start, and nose with specific widths and heights, planning to catmull-interpolate through them for a smooth lofted head shape.

For the lower jaw I'll switch to a frustumBox for that blocky Warcraft-style chunkiness, defining a jaw joint and tapering width/height from the hinge to the chin tip. I'm adding a small black sphere for the nose tip, cone-shaped fangs in both jaws, and amber spheres with dark pupils for the eyes.

I'm working out eye placement using the head's local coordinate system, mirroring left/right symmetrically with the model's own left/right convention rather than screen-space.

For the eye itself, I'll use an amber ellipsoid positioned at the brow ridge, checking skull width so the sphere sits just inside the surface without poking through too much. I'm also adding a small angled dark box above each eye as a brow wedge to get that angry, Warcraft-style look.

Actually, I'll build the brow as a rod between two points instead, since rod endpoints are flat and easier to position—using explicit local coordinates on the head joint. Since local() returns a plain Vector3 without bone attachment, I need to explicitly pass `bone: head` for every head detail to avoid it snapping to the wrong nearest joint like the jaw or neck. Next I'm planning the ears as extruded triangular shapes with thickness, standing erect on the head.

Still working out ear orientation vectors...

I'll simplify by skipping the outward lean and just tilting the ears back slightly, treating them as pointy cones like a stylized wolf ear. I'm also adding a darker inner-ear layer slightly offset forward, computing the thickness direction via the cross product of the ear's local axes.

That extends outward slightly, which works since both ears can share the same world-forward orientation regardless of side. I realize I can keep the same axis vectors for both ears and instead introduce asymmetry by mirroring the outline's x-coordinates based on side, giving the outer edge a straighter profile and inner edge a sloped one—mirroring this way flips winding order, but the extrusion loop should still close correctly either way.

Still shaping the ear outline... now positioning the ear base relative to the head bone and considering an outward tilt direction for the ear.

I'm also sketching the neck ruff and cheek fur tufts, planning ring-arranged spikes around the neck and jagged backward-pointing tufts along the cheek to give the wolf a more Warcraft-style mane and ruff.

Mapping out the jagged polygon vertices and tracing each edge to confirm the shape stays simple and non-self-intersecting as it winds from front to back around the bottom.

Actually I'll offset the tuft to 0.1 so it sits outside the skull surface rather than clipping. Now I'm planning the neck ruff as a ring of spikes around the neck, using a ring generator with tilt angled slightly backward so the spikes lean away from the forward direction while standing outward from the neck surface.

For the mane, I'm staggering two rings and alternating gray shades per spike to avoid a uniform spiky halo look, going for that chunky shaggy Warcraft feel instead. I'm also thinking through how to add dorsal spikes along the spine, using a path-following generator that samples points along the spine centerline and orients each spike to face upward based on the tangent direction.

I'll null-coalesce the bone value to avoid type issues. For dorsal fur, I'm considering scattering fur-tuft card textures across the back, shoulders, and tail to get a fluffy look, using a simple svg tuft shape in gray.

Now I'm working out the leg structure: four legs with shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw joints, using limb solvers with segment lengths for upper arm, forearm, and pastern to position the front paws correctly near ground level.

So 4 names gives shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw as the tip joint. I'll pass the limb's point array directly as the path since polylines accept point arrays with knots at those points, letting the sweep smooth the corners naturally. The front legs should parent off the spine's joint near the shoulders.

Hind legs parent off the hips at root. For leg tubes I'll sweep tapering radii along the chain, thicker near the shoulder and narrowing toward the paw. The paw itself gets a chunky scaled sphere positioned slightly forward and up, with small cone-shaped claw spikes added at the front for the toes.

Toe claws are three small cones with slight x-offsets at the front of the paw. I'm tuning the paw sphere's vertical placement so it just touches the ground plane without clipping through, sinking only slightly for contact realism. For the hind legs I need a proper digitigrade bend -- hip, then a forward-bending stifle (knee), then the hock angling back before reaching the pastern, unlike the straighter front leg.

For the hind limb I'm planning three segments (roughly 0.30, 0.28, 0.2 long) bending knee-forward then hock-back, with the final metatarsus segment running vertical from the hock down to the foot target to get that classic wolf stance, and adjusting the hind foot's z-position further back than the hip to make the hock sit properly behind the line of the leg.

I also want to make sure the hip joints stay inside the body hull's width, and add haunch and shoulder muscle blobs (scaled ellipsoids) near the hip and shoulder joints to give the legs a chunkier, more muscular look.

Now I'm sketching the tail as a chain of points hanging from the hips, bushy in the middle with a dark tip, curving down and slightly outward for that alert wolf posture.

Still planning radius bands and tip coloring... I'm thinking through the coat paint scheme with countershading for a gray-blue back and cream underside/muzzle, giving it that Warcraft-style contrast.

Now I'm working out the body loft with the spine bone chain, making sure stations outside the chain's range still get skinned properly to the nearest endpoint joint.

Defining more loft stations...

Adding ears and head puts total height around 1.3, bigger than a real wolf but fitting a Warcraft-style, dire-wolf proportion. I'll accept the larger stylized scale rather than rescale the whole rig.

Now I'm working through the body loft and skeleton setup, chaining the spine bones for skinning, then sweeping the neck geometry from the body's end point into the neck base coordinates.

I'm laying out skull stations relative to the head joint — back skull, brow, mid-muzzle, and nose, sizing each with rough width and height to match the wolf's forehead-stop-muzzle profile. I think it'd be cleaner to define these from head.local orientation words rather than raw coordinates for consistency.

Defining head helper function...

Adjusting the jaw geometry to keep the mouth closed with the lower jaw tucked behind the upper, then adding small fang spikes jutting downward from the muzzle sides for a bit of character detail.

Repositioning the nose closer to the muzzle tip and confirming bone roles for jaw, head, neck, and spine. Now I'm working out the eye placement and sizing, figuring out the skull width at that forward position to keep them properly nested within the head geometry.

I'm placing a small dark pupil slightly forward and outward from each eye sphere, then starting on the brow ridge geometry—angling it so the inner ends slope down toward the nose for a fierce, angry expression while the outer ends lift higher.

Checking these coordinates against the skull's ellipsoid shape to make sure the eyes sit mid-height along its side and the brows trace properly along its upper surface.

I'll settle on inner brow point around (0.13, 0.125) and outer around (0.07, 0.09), colored dark-gray, skipping muzzle bridge, dorsal tuft, eye decals, and whiskers for now. Moving to body details, I'm planning a cream chest blaze using an ellipsoid shape at the chest front.

Still working out the cream fur coverage though -- I'll use rings of spikes around the lower neck instead, angled downward to cover the underside and chest area, with a main neck ruff ring of larger tilted spikes for volume.

For the gray secondary ring, I'll cycle through a few shades per spike for texture variation. I'm also working out how tilt interacts with the ring's facing direction -- negative tilt should lean spikes backward along the neck's tangent toward the body, which is what I want for a natural lay-down look.

Now I'm thinking about dorsal spines running along the spine chain from the rump to the shoulders, positioning each spike's base on the body's centerline but offset upward since the body's cross-sectional height varies along that path -- thinner near the tail root and fuller near the shoulders.

Instead of hardcoding offsets, I'm reconsidering a ray-casting approach: shooting rays down onto the body mesh at each spine position to find the actual surface hits, then sticking cone-shaped spikes oriented along the surface normal at each point, with some embed depth so they're anchored properly. The challenge is getting the fur to sweep backward rather than pointing straight up along the normal, since the stick function's flow parameter only biases in one fixed direction.

Spikes along the dorsal ridge use a backward-leaning direction vector rather than the surface normal, with sizes tapering larger near the shoulders to form a mane-like crest, alternating with dark charcoal coloring. I'm now considering using SVG tuft cards across the body surface for additional fur texture, starting to define the viewBox dimensions for that shape.

I'm shaping each tuft as a simple pointed leaf-like path drawn in white, which gets tinted by the part's color string at render time so a single greyscale drawing can take on any coat color. I'm planning around 260 cards scattered across the body, excluding the belly area, with triangular geometry, two-sided rendering, slight lean and bend, and a backward flow direction to mimic combed fur.

I'm estimating triangle counts for the fur cards and deciding to skip adding extra tail or haunch tufts for now since the tail tip and body coverage already handle those areas visually. I'm settling on using the coat paint directly for the card color without extra tinting tricks.

Now I'm adding shoulder muscle blobs as scaled sphere parts attached to the shoulder joint, using the coat paint with countershading, and considering whether the non-uniform scaling will distort the surface normals in a way that affects the shading.

I'm checking the leg geometry: the front leg root sits slightly inside the chest wall so the thick leg radius pokes outward for a chunky look, and I'm nudging the foot position to splay slightly outward for a more natural stance. Then I'm working through whether the leg root height is too high relative to the total chain length, since the reach from hip to foot is less than the fully extended leg length, meaning the knee/elbow needs to bend backward to avoid the leg looking overstretched or buckled.

Testing segment lengths for a mostly-straight wolf foreleg, I find that equal 0.3+0.3 segments force a large 0.19 elbow bend, which looks too kinked, so I try shorter segments like 0.26/0.24/0.1 that leave the limb almost straight with only a small 0.07 bend -- much more natural. Now I'm moving to the hind leg, setting up similar segment proportions to compute the thigh bend from the hip root down to the paw target.

Hind toes use the same paw design. Checking the hip x-coordinate—the limb plane through root, target, and hint works fine, with s=1 mapping to left (L) and s=-1 to right (R).

Now I'm writing a paw construction function that places an ellipsoid at the leg's tip joint, sized and positioned for the foot, and figuring out an appropriate dark tan fur color for the paws.

For the leg coat, I'm defining color gradients along the vertical axis so the leg fades from the main coat color to the darker paw tone. Then I'm adding three small claw spikes at the toe positions, offset in x and attached to the paw joint with a claw color.

Rather than risky groove rods on the ellipsoid surface, I'll skip those and instead add three small toe-bump ellipsoids scaled slightly for a chunky look, positioned near the front of the paw with claws starting just past them.

I'm adding backward-pointing fur-tuft spikes at the elbow and hock joints for a stylized Warcraft-like spur effect, plus some spikes at the tail root, while skipping dewclaws and eye glow. For the ears I'm going with gray outer surfaces and a darker pinkish-brown inner color for contrast.

Now I'm defining the color palette—grays, char, cream, amber, nose black, ivory, and claw tones—and setting up the paint functions, using a mottled base texture combined with a countershade effect to give the coat natural light-to-dark gradation across the body.

I'm layering a second countershade on top to create a darker saddle marking across the back where surfaces face upward, nesting the gradient so the saddle sits over the lighter underlying coat tone.

Now I'm setting up the tail with a sweep gradient using the base coat color, adding bands near the tip so the last portion darkens to the charcoal tip color.

Next I want to give the tail some bushiness with varying radii along its length, plus fur card scatter on both body and tail surfaces for texture, keeping the pose a simple neutral hang.

For the hind legs, I'm setting up thicker thigh radii that taper down toward the paw, with joints spaced along the leg path so the limb reads as sturdy at the hip and narrower lower down -- rounding the joints to avoid sharp polyline breaks. I also want to check the lowest points of the model, like paw bottoms and tail tip, to make sure everything sits properly on the floor plane.

Checking total height against the head and ear tips confirms the proportions are within a reasonable tolerance, so I'm satisfied with the overall scale. For the spheres I'll use flat shading with a low-poly sphere geometry, and I'll skip extra details like whiskers, eyebrow lids, and nostril dots since the nose ellipsoid already conveys that area -- same with skipping a separate mouth line since the muzzle geometry isn't well-defined enough to loft one cleanly.

Now I'm working out fur card placement: using the card-scattering function with hit frames from the body surface, filtering by normal direction so cards lean backward and avoid the leg blobs, then building out the ears by positioning them relative to the skull's local coordinate frame, checking that the base height and forward offset line up with the brow and back-skull measurements I worked out earlier.

Now I'm fitting the ear's outline and inner-ear shape by tracing coordinates so the inner outline stays nested within the outer ear shape, adjusting edge points to keep thickness and taper consistent along the ear's length.

I'll keep the inner ear color at "#7a5a52" with no bevel taper, and account for the sign flip on the thickness offset so the ear's front face sits properly relative to the base depth.

Checking the inner-to-outer thickness taper against the ear's own curvature, the inner surface stays comfortably inside the ear shape at the midpoint height without poking through. The ear also tilts backward slightly as height increases, so I'm adjusting the forward axis accordingly.

Now I'm adding cheek tufts with a lighter cream-grey color, keeping it to just one tuft rather than stacking a second smaller one, and planning dark brow tufts plus a forehead crest next.

For the head crest, I'll add 2-3 small spikes along the top, pointing back and up, positioned near the brow line for that Warcraft-style silhouette. Then I'm setting up the neck chain parented to the spine with a defined role, and building the spine chain itself from a catmull-rom curve through the hip joints.

The spine curve's five points generate four spans and four joints, with the hips acting as the root joint at the first point, overlapping cleanly with the spine chain's start. The neck uses a three-point curve for two spans, while the tail uses a five-point curve parented to the hips for four tail joints.

I'm defining the jaw joint parented to the head with aim direction set for articulation, and the head joint itself parented to the second neck joint using its frame position and a slight downward-forward direction. Front legs will parent to the fourth spine joint positioned further back along the body.

Now I'm adding small spike details at the elbow and hock joints to suggest bony protrusions, sized to peek out from under the leg tubes without clipping too much, plus a haunch ellipsoid positioned near the hips to flesh out the hind leg silhouette.

I'm checking that the shoulder and haunch blobs sit within the body's bounds without poking too far outside the back line, then setting up the loft call for the main body surface using the spine as the bone reference, trusting that sweep-returning shorthand works with the surface function.

Now I'm verifying the handoff points between the body loft, neck sweep, and skull loft - matching radii across the neck tube and checking that the circle cross-sections at each joint roughly line up with the hull widths so there's no visible gap or mismatch where the neck meets the body and head.

Starting to draft the actual build script: setting up imports from the builder SDK, confirming paint helpers like mottle, countershade, and gradient come from the same module, then laying out the root hips joint and beginning the spine chain with catmull-spline control points, deciding to skip the "spine" role on the root joint itself to avoid duplicate role conflicts with the chain.

Now I'm working out the leg construction loop, mirroring left and right sides and defining shoulder and foot target positions with limb() bend directions for elbow and wrist joints, adjusting the front foot's forward offset slightly to keep the stance looking alert and straight underneath the body.

I'm wiring up the chain call with named joints and a contact point, then sweeping the leg with a tapered radius gradient, and sketching out a paw-building function that adds a foot pad sphere plus three toe spheres with claws attached to the final leg bone.

Positioning the paw and toes relative to the leg's end point, then setting up a hind leg target and starting the tail as a catmull-rom spline chain parented to the hips.

Defining tail sweep radii with tapering toward a pointed tip, color banding toward a tail-tip color, and checking that the tube stays sized appropriately near the body.

Now I'm working on scattering fur tuft textures across the body and neck surfaces, generating a simple leaf-shaped tuft SVG and setting up the scatter parameters with minimum distance and a normal-based filter to control placement density.

For the tail, I'm setting up a separate scatter pass of around 80 cards along the tail sweep, filtering by surface normal, and then applying cards with coat coloring mixed in.

For dorsal spikes, I'm casting downward rays along the spine at intervals to find surface hit points, then placing spikes at each hit scaled by position along the row.

For spike sizing, I'm making them bigger around the withers and tapering length by position, embedding the cone base flush at the surface hit so it reads as attached. Then I'm setting up neck ruff rings along a chain point and starting on head spikes and eye/pupil placement with a mirrored helper function.

Working through eye placement using the head's local coordinate helper, then considering a tiny highlight sphere for the eye glint, skipping nostrils and whiskers, and adding a cheek tuft positioned slightly back from the skull with a grayish color.

I'm defining the ear outline as a typed tuple array and setting up loft stations with position, width, and height, keeping the body parts like waist, scruff pad, and belly minimal for now before moving on to the hind leg thigh.

Now I'm adding Warcraft-style shoulder spikes as bony fur spurs, placing their base inside the shoulder blob and computing direction and length so they emerge visibly beyond the blob's radius.

I'm deciding to skip war-paint and collar details as unnecessary, confirming the jaw rig and forearm spike chains are already handled, then finalizing the limb function usage and setting up a gradient paint for the leg fur sweeps.

For the hind legs I'll use a similar coat-to-paw-color gradient but shifted slightly lower, and apply the same coat gradients to the paws, toes, and body blobs. I'm also adjusting the head loft coloring so the muzzle fades to cream while keeping a darker saddle tone across the top of the head.

Now I'm setting up small flat sphere geometries for the eyes, then looping over left/right symmetry to extrude each ear with a coat-colored outer surface, defining its position, orientation, and taper thickness relative to the head bone.

Spike-based teeth with ivory color, and a rod for eyebrows, keeping the stance mostly symmetric with slightly forward front legs. I'm also checking the jaw box dimensions by comparing coordinates for the upper and lower jaw frustums to make sure the mouth geometry lines up before finalizing and returning the root.

I realize the lower fangs end up hidden entirely inside the muzzle volume, so they're pointless but not harmful; I consider lowering the jaw slightly so the teeth would actually be visible.

Opening the jaw by a 10-12° hinge rotation gives that alert wolf look with fangs showing, which seems like a nice touch even though it slightly shortens the forward extent. I decide a small open-mouth pose is better than fully neutral, and briefly consider adding a small pink tongue box inside the jaw, though a dark mouth interior isn't really necessary.

Then I run through the geometry for the lower fangs with the jaw opened at various angles, checking whether the fang tips would actually clear the muzzle bottom and be visible through the gap -- at 12° they stay mostly hidden, and even lengthening them or opening to 20° only barely exposes them, so I'm working through the math to find an angle that actually reveals the fangs.

That settles the proportions. For colors, the lower jaw gets a plain cream tone while the upper muzzle uses a cream gradient, and I need to make sure no unused variables cause issues before writing the final code.
